probable_causes: The database server is down, restarting, or not listening on the expected port.
Wrong host, port, database name, or credentials in the deployed configuration.
A firewall, security group, or network rule blocks the application from reaching the database.
The connection pool is exhausted or the database has reached its maximum connections.
diagnostic_checks: Confirm the database service is running and healthy from the database host's monitoring or status page.
Verify the host, port, and database name in the deployed configuration match the intended environment.
Test network reachability from the application server to the database host and port using your approved network tools.
Check whether the credentials used by the application are valid and not expired or rotated.
corrective_actions: Correct the database connection settings (host, port, credentials) in the configuration for this environment.
Ask the network or security team to allow traffic from the application server to the database port if it is blocked.
Review connection pool size and the database's maximum connection limit with the database administrator.
Re-run the deployment only after connectivity is confirmed.
validation_steps: The application starts and its health check reports the database connection as healthy.
A simple read query from the application succeeds.
No new connection errors appear in the logs for several minutes.

probable_causes: A required package or library is missing from the requirements or lock file.
The requested package version does not exist or conflicts with another package.
The package registry or artifact repository is unreachable or the package was removed.
The runtime version (Python, Node, Java) is incompatible with the package.
diagnostic_checks: Compare the missing package name and version with the project's requirements or lock file.
Check that the package registry or artifact repository is reachable from the build or deployment server.
Verify the runtime version on the server matches the version the project expects.
Look for conflicting version constraints reported in the log.
corrective_actions: Add the missing dependency to the requirements or lock file with a version that exists and is compatible.
Resolve version conflicts by aligning package versions, then regenerate the lock file.
Configure access to the correct package registry or mirror if it is unreachable.
Rebuild the deployment package after fixing the dependency list.
validation_steps: The dependency installation step completes without errors.
The application starts and imports the previously missing package.
The build produces the same dependency versions in every environment.

probable_causes: A configuration file has a syntax error such as bad indentation, a stray bracket, or a duplicate key.
A setting has an invalid value or an unknown property for this application version.
The configuration for another environment was deployed by mistake.
A configured port is already used by another process.
diagnostic_checks: Open the file and line number named in the log and look for syntax mistakes.
Compare the failing configuration with the last known working version in version control.
Check whether the configured port is already used by another service.
Confirm the configuration matches the target environment.
corrective_actions: Fix the syntax or invalid value and validate the file with the appropriate linter or the application's built-in config check.
Revert to the last known good configuration through your normal change process if the cause is unclear.
Change the conflicting port setting or stop the competing service through the approved process.
Redeploy with the corrected configuration.
validation_steps: The application starts and parses its configuration without errors.
The service listens on the expected port.
A smoke test of the main feature passes.

probable_causes: A code change introduced a syntax or type error that prevents compilation.
A build script, task, or test step failed.
The build environment differs from the developer environment (tool or SDK version).
A missing generated file or an incomplete checkout.
diagnostic_checks: Find the first error in the build output; later errors are often a consequence of it.
Check which commit introduced the failure and what changed.
Compare the build tool and SDK versions on the build server with the project's expected versions.
Re-run the failing build step and compare the result.
corrective_actions: Fix the code error reported at the file and line shown in the log.
Align the build tool or SDK version with the project's required version.
Fix or update the failing build script or test, then commit the change.
Trigger a new build from a clean workspace.
validation_steps: The build completes successfully and produces the expected artifact.
All automated tests in the pipeline pass.
The artifact deploys to a test environment.

probable_causes: The deployment user or service account lacks the required file, folder, or role permissions.
A recent permission, role, or policy change removed access.
A script is not marked as executable.
Credentials or tokens used by the pipeline have expired or have too few privileges.
diagnostic_checks: Identify the exact user or role and the exact resource named in the error.
Check the permissions of that resource and compare them with what the deployment needs.
Review recent access or policy changes for the account.
Confirm the pipeline's credentials are still valid.
corrective_actions: Request the minimum required permission for the deployment account through your access-management process.
Fix the ownership or executable permission of the specific file with the system administrator's approval.
Renew expired credentials using the approved secret-management process.
Avoid granting broad permissions as a quick fix.
validation_steps: The previously failing step now succeeds with the least-privileged account.
No new permission errors appear in the logs.
The permission change is recorded in the change log.

probable_causes: The new version is slow to start or fails its health check, so the rollout never completes.
A dependency (database, API) the service waits for is slow or unavailable.
The timeout setting is too short for the application's normal startup time.
Resource shortages slow down the deployment.
diagnostic_checks: Check the application's own startup logs for the service that timed out.
Check that the health check or readiness endpoint is correct and reachable.
Verify the services this application depends on are healthy.
Compare current startup time with previous successful deployments.
corrective_actions: Fix the startup or health-check problem shown in the application logs.
Restore any unhealthy dependency through its owning team.
Increase the timeout only if the normal startup time is legitimately longer, and record the reason.
Roll back through your approved release process if the service is impacted.
validation_steps: The rollout completes and the service reports healthy.
Startup time is within the expected range.
Traffic is served without gateway or timeout errors.

probable_causes: The process or container memory limit is too low for the workload.
The disk or volume is full (logs, old releases, temporary files).
The cluster has no free CPU or memory to schedule the new instance.
A memory leak or a file or connection leak in the application.
diagnostic_checks: Check memory, CPU, and disk usage on the affected host or container in your monitoring tool.
Compare the configured resource limits with the actual usage.
Check for large or old files, such as logs and old releases, consuming disk space.
Check whether usage grows steadily over time, which suggests a leak.
corrective_actions: Increase the memory, CPU, or disk allocation through the approved change process.
Clean up unneeded files according to your retention policy, with the owner's approval.
Add cluster capacity or reduce the requested resources if scheduling fails.
Open a defect to investigate suspected leaks.
validation_steps: Resource usage stays below the limits during and after deployment.
The application runs without out-of-memory or disk errors.
Monitoring alerts for resources are clear.

probable_causes: A required variable was not defined for this environment in the pipeline or hosting platform.
The variable name is misspelled or differs between environments.
A secret store or variable group was not linked to this deployment.
A new version of the application requires a variable that was not added to the environment.
diagnostic_checks: Note the exact variable name in the log and check whether it is defined for this environment.
Compare the variables of the failing environment with a working one.
Check the release notes or configuration template for newly required variables.
Check that the secret store or variable group is linked to the deployment.
corrective_actions: Define the missing variable in the deployment platform or secret store using the approved process.
Correct the variable name if it is misspelled.
Update the environment template or documentation so the variable is not forgotten again.
Redeploy after confirming all required variables are set.
validation_steps: The application starts without missing-variable errors.
The feature that depends on the variable works.
The variable list matches the documented template.
